lessons.title: Cell Structure and Microscopy
lessons.description: Eukaryotic vs prokaryotic cells, organelle functions, specialisation and microscopy.
lessons.content_html:
Eukaryotic and Prokaryotic Cells

All living things are made of cells. Cells are divided into two fundamental types: eukaryotic cells and prokaryotic cells. Understanding the differences between these two types is a key part of AQA and regularly tested in exams.

Eukaryotic cells include both animal and plant cells. They have a nucleus that encloses their genetic material, along with other membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells — bacteria — are much smaller and simpler. They lack a true nucleus: instead, their genetic material is a single loop of DNA that floats freely in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes may also contain small rings of extra DNA called plasmids.

Key Fact

Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a nucleus that encloses their DNA. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus — their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, and they may also contain plasmids.

A typical animal cell is around 10–30 µm (micrometres) in diameter. A prokaryotic bacterial cell is much smaller, typically 1–5 µm. You need to be comfortable with order of magnitude calculations using standard form, and the prefixes centi (10−2), milli (10−3), micro (10−6) and nano (10−9).

Animal and Plant Cells

Both animal and plant cells are eukaryotic, but they contain different organelles. You must be able to name each organelle and explain how its structure relates to its function.

Nucleus — contains the cell’s genetic material (DNA) and controls the cell’s activities. The DNA carries the instructions for making proteins.

Cytoplasm — a jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions take place. Enzymes in the cytoplasm control these metabolic reactions.

Cell membrane — a thin layer that surrounds the cell and controls which substances enter and leave. It is selectively permeable.

Mitochondria — the site of aerobic respiration, where energy is transferred from glucose. Cells that need lots of energy (such as muscle cells) contain more mitochondria.

Ribosomes — tiny structures in the cytoplasm where protein synthesis occurs. They are found in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.

Plant cells have all of the organelles listed above, plus three additional structures:

Chloroplasts — contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. They absorb light energy to make glucose.

Permanent vacuole — a large, fluid-filled space containing cell sap (a weak solution of sugars and salts). It helps keep the cell rigid and supports the plant.

Cell wall — made of cellulose and surrounds the cell membrane. It strengthens and supports the cell, preventing it from bursting when water enters by osmosis.

Key Fact

Plant cells have a cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a permanent vacuole (cell sap) in addition to the organelles found in animal cells. Bacterial cells have a cell wall but no chloroplasts, no true nucleus and no mitochondria.

Cell Specialisation

Not every cell in an organism looks the same. Cells become specialised — they develop particular structures that allow them to perform a specific function. The exam regularly asks you to explain how a cell’s structure relates to its function.

Sperm cell — has a streamlined head, a long tail (flagellum) for swimming, and many mitochondria to provide energy for movement. It carries the male DNA to the egg.

Nerve cell — has a long axon to carry electrical impulses over long distances, branched endings (dendrites) to connect with other nerve cells, and a myelin sheath to insulate the signal and speed up transmission.

Muscle cell — contains many mitochondria to supply energy for contraction. Muscle cells are elongated so they can contract and relax to produce movement.

Root hair cell — has a long, thin extension (the root hair) that increases the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.

Xylem cell — a hollow, dead tube reinforced with lignin that transports water and mineral ions from roots to leaves in a continuous column.

Phloem cell — has sieve plates with pores that allow dissolved sugars to flow through the plant from leaves to other parts (translocation).

Cell Differentiation

The process by which a cell becomes specialised is called differentiation. As a cell differentiates, it acquires the sub-cellular structures it needs for its function.

Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage of development. Once they have specialised, they generally cannot change into a different cell type, and cell division in mature animals is mainly for repair and replacement. Plant cells, however, retain the ability to differentiate throughout their lives. This is why you can take a cutting from a plant and it will grow into a new individual.

Key Fact

Animal cells differentiate early and are then permanently specialised. Plant cells can differentiate throughout life — this is why cuttings can grow into new plants.

Microscopy

Microscopes allow us to see cells and sub-cellular structures that are invisible to the naked eye. There are two main types you need to know about: light microscopes and electron microscopes.

Light microscopes use glass lenses and visible light to produce a magnified image. They have a maximum useful magnification of about ×1,500 and a resolution (the ability to distinguish two close points as separate) of around 200 nm. Light microscopes were first developed in the 1590s and allowed scientists to discover cells for the first time.

Electron microscopes fire a beam of electrons at the specimen rather than using light. They have a much higher resolution (down to about 0.2 nm) and a useful magnification of up to ×2,000,000. This allows biologists to see sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and the internal structure of mitochondria in much finer detail.

You must be able to use the magnification formula:

\(magnification = \text{size of image} \div \text{size of real object}\)

This can be rearranged using a formula triangle. If the image of a cell is 30 mm across and the real cell is 0.03 mm (30 µm), then: magnification = 30 ÷ 0.03 = ×1,000. Always check both measurements are in the same units before dividing. Express very large or very small answers in standard form where appropriate.

Required Practical 1 asks you to use a light microscope to observe, draw and label plant and animal cells, including a magnification scale on your drawing. To prepare a slide, you place a thin sample on a glass slide, add a drop of water or stain (such as iodine), and lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid trapping air bubbles. You then view the slide starting on the lowest magnification objective and focus using the coarse and fine adjustment knobs.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on cell structure, always link the organelle to its function — for example, “mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration.” In magnification calculations, the most common mistake is forgetting to convert units so that both image size and real size are in the same unit (usually mm or µm) before dividing. Show every step of your working for full marks on “Calculate” questions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus and contain plasmids.
  • Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole in addition to the organelles in animal cells.
  • Cells specialise through differentiation — animal cells differentiate early, plant cells can differentiate throughout life.
  • Electron microscopes have higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes, and the magnification formula is: magnification = image size ÷ real size.

lessons.title: Cell Division and Transport
lessons.description: How cells divide by mitosis and how substances move in and out of cells.
lessons.content_html:
Chromosomes and the Genetic Material

The nucleus of every cell contains thread-like structures called chromosomes. Each chromosome is a long molecule of DNA, and each chromosome carries a large number of genes. In body cells, chromosomes are found in pairs — human body cells contain 23 pairs, giving 46 chromosomes in total.

Key Fact

Human body cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in total). Each chromosome is made of DNA and carries many genes.

The Cell Cycle and Mitosis

Cells divide in a series of stages called the cell cycle. The cell cycle allows organisms to grow, repair damaged tissue, and replace worn-out cells. Before a cell divides, it must prepare by growing larger and increasing the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria. The DNA then replicates so that each chromosome is copied, producing two identical copies.

The stage of the cell cycle where the cell actually divides its nucleus is called mitosis. During mitosis, one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides. Finally, the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to form two identical daughter cells. Each new cell has exactly the same number of chromosomes — and exactly the same genetic information — as the original parent cell.

Stage 1 — Growth and DNA replication: The cell grows, increases the number of sub-cellular structures (e.g. mitochondria, ribosomes), and the DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.

Stage 2 — Mitosis: One set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides into two.

Stage 3 — Division: The cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to produce two identical daughter cells. In plant cells, a new cell wall also forms.

Key Fact

You need to know the three overall stages of the cell cycle, but you do not need to name the individual phases of mitosis (prophase, metaphase, etc.).

Stem Cells

A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to produce many more cells of the same type. Certain stem cells can also differentiate into specialised cell types. There are three main sources of stem cells that The specification requires you to know.

Embryonic stem cells are found in early human embryos. They can differentiate into almost any type of human cell, making them extremely useful for medical research. Adult stem cells are found in bone marrow and can form many types of cells, including blood cells, but they are more limited than embryonic stem cells. Meristem tissue in plants contains stem cells that can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the plant’s life.

Medical uses: Stem cell treatments may help conditions such as diabetes and paralysis. In therapeutic cloning, an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient, so stem cells from it are not rejected by the patient’s immune system.

Risks: There is a potential risk of transferring viral infections through stem cell treatments.

Ethical objections: Some people object to embryonic stem cell research because it involves the destruction of a human embryo, which they consider to be a potential human life. Others argue the potential to save lives justifies the research.

Plant stem cells: Meristem cells can be used to produce clones of plants quickly and economically. This is used to clone rare species to protect them from extinction and to produce large numbers of crop plants with desirable features such as disease resistance.

Diffusion

Diffusion is the spreading out of particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. It is a passive process — it does not require energy from the cell.

Important examples of diffusion in biology include oxygen and carbon dioxide moving in and out of cells during gas exchange, and the waste product urea moving from cells into the blood plasma for excretion by the kidneys.

Key Fact

Three factors affect the rate of diffusion: the concentration gradient (difference in concentration), the temperature, and the surface area of the membrane.

A single-celled organism has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio, allowing sufficient transport of molecules by diffusion alone. Multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces (such as the lungs, small intestine, gills, roots, and leaves) because their surface area to volume ratio is much smaller relative to their needs. These exchange surfaces are adapted by having a large surface area, thin membranes for a short diffusion path, a rich blood supply, and ventilation.

Osmosis

Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution (where water molecules are in higher concentration) to a concentrated solution (where water molecules are in lower concentration) through a partially permeable membrane. Like diffusion, osmosis is a passive process and does not require energy from respiration.

AQA Required Practical 3 involves investigating the effect of a range of concentrations of salt or sugar solutions on the mass of plant tissue (usually potato cylinders). You measure the mass before and after placing the tissue in each solution, then calculate percentage change in mass. In dilute solutions, the tissue gains mass by osmosis (water enters the cells). In concentrated solutions, it loses mass (water leaves the cells). You should be able to plot and interpret graphs of percentage mass change against solution concentration.

Active Transport

Active transport moves substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution — this means it works against the concentration gradient. Unlike diffusion and osmosis, active transport requires energy from respiration.

There are two key examples the specification requires. First, active transport allows mineral ions to be absorbed into plant root hair cells from very dilute solutions in the soil — plants need these minerals for healthy growth. Second, it allows sugar molecules to be absorbed from the gut into the blood, even though the blood already has a higher sugar concentration than the gut contents. The sugar is then used for cell respiration.

Key Fact

The three transport processes compared: Diffusion — high to low concentration, passive (no energy). Osmosis — water only, dilute to concentrated through a partially permeable membrane, passive. Active transport — low to high concentration (against the gradient), requires energy from respiration.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on transport in cells, always state the direction of movement relative to the concentration gradient. For diffusion and osmosis, say “from high to low concentration” (or “dilute to concentrated” for osmosis). For active transport, say “against the concentration gradient” and mention that it “requires energy from respiration.” A common mistake is confusing osmosis with diffusion — remember, osmosis is specifically the movement of water through a partially permeable membrane. In 6-mark extended response questions, always compare the three processes using a clear structure: name, direction, energy requirement, and a biological example.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The cell cycle consists of three stages: growth and DNA replication, mitosis (nuclear division), and cytoplasm/membrane division — producing two genetically identical daughter cells.
  • Stem cells (embryonic, adult, and plant meristem) are undifferentiated cells that can divide and specialise — they have medical potential but raise ethical concerns.
  • Substances move in and out of cells by diffusion (passive, high to low), osmosis (water through a partially permeable membrane, passive), and active transport (against the gradient, requires energy from respiration).

lessons.title: Organisation and the Digestive System
lessons.description: How enzymes, bile, and digestive organs break down food into absorbable molecules.
lessons.content_html:
Principles of Organisation

The human body is organised into a hierarchy of structures, each more complex than the last. Cells are the basic building blocks of all living organisms. A group of cells with a similar structure and function is called a tissue. Tissues are grouped together to form organs, and organs are organised into organ systems.

The digestive system is a perfect example of an organ system — several different organs work together to digest food and absorb the nutrients the body needs. Understanding this hierarchy (cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism) is essential for AQA Biology, as it shows how the body is organised to carry out complex functions efficiently.

Key Fact

The hierarchy of organisation in the body is: \(cells \rightarrow tissues \rightarrow organs \rightarrow \text{organ systems} \rightarrow organism\). The digestive system is an organ system in which the stomach, small intestine, pancreas, liver, and other organs work together to break down and absorb food.

The Human Digestive System

The role of the digestive system is to break down large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream and transported to cells. This process involves both mechanical digestion (physical breakdown by chewing and churning) and chemical digestion (breakdown by enzymes).

The digestive system includes the following organs, each with a specific role:

Mouth: Food is chewed into smaller pieces (mechanical digestion) and mixed with saliva, which contains the enzyme amylase. This begins the chemical digestion of starch into sugars.

Oesophagus: A muscular tube that pushes food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis (waves of muscle contraction).

Stomach: A muscular organ that churns food and mixes it with hydrochloric acid and protease enzymes. The acid kills bacteria and provides the acidic pH (around pH 2) that stomach proteases need to work.

Small intestine: Where the final stages of chemical digestion occur and where the products of digestion are absorbed into the bloodstream. The inner wall is covered in tiny finger-like projections called villi, which increase the surface area for absorption.

Large intestine: Absorbs water from undigested food, forming solid faeces.

Pancreas: A gland that produces protease, lipase, and amylase enzymes, which are released into the small intestine.

Liver: Produces bile, which is stored in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine.

Enzymes and Digestion

Digestive enzymes are biological catalysts — they speed up the breakdown of large food molecules without being used up themselves. Each enzyme has a specifically shaped active site that fits only one type of substrate, like a lock and key. This is called the lock and key theory.

There are three main groups of digestive enzymes, and you must know what each one does, where it is produced, and what it breaks food down into:

Key Fact

Amylase (a carbohydrase) breaks down starch into simple sugars (maltose/glucose). It is produced in the salivary glands, the pancreas, and the small intestine.

Key Fact

Proteases break down proteins into amino acids. They are produced in the stomach (pepsin, which works best in acidic conditions), the pancreas, and the small intestine.

Key Fact

Lipases break down lipids (fats and oils) into glycerol and fatty acids. They are produced in the pancreas and the small intestine.

The Role of Bile

Bile plays a crucial role in digestion, even though it is not an enzyme. It is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. When food enters the small intestine, bile is released and has two important functions:

1. Neutralisation: Bile is alkaline, so it neutralises the hydrochloric acid that comes from the stomach. This is important because enzymes in the small intestine work best in slightly alkaline conditions (around pH 7–8). Without bile, the acid from the stomach would make the pH too low for these enzymes to function.

2. Emulsification of fats: Bile emulsifies fats — it breaks large fat globules into much smaller droplets. This massively increases the surface area of the fat, giving lipase enzymes a much larger area to work on. This speeds up the rate of fat digestion.

Enzymes can only work on the surface of food molecules. When bile breaks large fat globules into tiny droplets, the total surface area exposed to lipase increases dramatically. Think of it like this: a whole block of butter has a small surface area, but if you broke it into thousands of tiny pieces, the combined surface area would be far greater. More surface area means more lipase molecules can bind to fat at the same time, so digestion happens much faster.

Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity

Enzymes are proteins, and their activity is affected by temperature and pH. Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH at which it works fastest.

If the temperature is too low, molecules move slowly and collide with the active site less frequently, so the reaction rate is low. As temperature increases, molecules move faster and collide more often, increasing the rate. At the optimum temperature (around 37°C for most human enzymes), the rate is at its maximum.

If the temperature rises above the optimum, the enzyme’s active site changes shape — the enzyme is denatured. The substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme can no longer catalyse the reaction. Denaturation is permanent.

Similarly, extreme changes in pH can denature enzymes. Stomach protease (pepsin) works best at pH 2 (very acidic), while enzymes in the small intestine work best at around pH 7–8 (slightly alkaline). This is why bile’s role in neutralising stomach acid is so important.

AQA Required Practical 5 asks you to investigate how pH affects the rate of amylase activity. You add amylase to a starch solution at different pH values (using buffer solutions) and sample the mixture every 30 seconds using iodine reagent. Iodine turns blue-black in the presence of starch. When the iodine no longer changes colour, all the starch has been digested. You record the time taken at each pH and use it to calculate the rate of reaction (rate = 1 ÷ time). A water bath is used to keep the temperature constant so that pH is the only variable being tested.

Products of Digestion

Once food has been fully digested, the small, soluble molecules are absorbed through the walls of the small intestine into the bloodstream. These products are then used by the body:

Simple sugars (glucose) are used in respiration to release energy, or converted into starch, glycogen, or cellulose for storage. Amino acids are used to build new proteins for growth and repair. Glycerol and fatty acids are used to build new lipid molecules for cell membranes and energy storage.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In AQA Trilogy exams, enzyme questions are very common. Always name the specific enzyme, the substrate it acts on, and the products formed (e.g. “Lipase breaks down lipids into glycerol and fatty acids”). For bile questions, remember that bile is not an enzyme — it emulsifies fats and neutralises acid. If asked about factors affecting enzyme activity, explain why using the lock and key model: at high temperatures, the active site changes shape (denatures), so the substrate no longer fits.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The digestive system is organised as cells → tissues → organs → organ systems. The stomach, small intestine, pancreas, and liver all work together to digest and absorb food.
  • Three enzyme groups do the chemical work: amylase (starch → sugars), proteases (proteins → amino acids), and lipases (lipids → glycerol + fatty acids). Know where each is produced.
  • Bile is not an enzyme — it neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fats to increase surface area for lipase, speeding up fat digestion.

lessons.title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease
lessons.description: Heart structure, blood vessels, blood components, and coronary heart disease treatments.
lessons.content_html:
The Double Circulatory System

The human body uses a double circulatory system. This means blood passes through the heart twice during each full circuit. One loop carries blood from the heart to the lungs and back (the pulmonary circuit), where oxygen is picked up and carbon dioxide is removed. The second loop carries oxygenated blood from the heart to the rest of the body and returns deoxygenated blood back to the heart (the systemic circuit).

A double circulatory system is more efficient than a single one because blood returning from the lungs is pumped a second time by the heart before reaching body tissues. This maintains high pressure, ensuring organs receive oxygen quickly enough for aerobic respiration.

Key Fact

In a double circulatory system, blood enters the heart twice on each journey around the body: once from the lungs (oxygenated) and once from the body (deoxygenated).

Structure of the Heart

The heart is a muscular organ divided into four chambers. The two upper chambers are called the atria (singular: atrium) and the two lower chambers are the ventricles. The right side of the heart handles deoxygenated blood, while the left side handles oxygenated blood. Valves between the chambers prevent blood from flowing backwards.

The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle because it needs to pump blood at high pressure all the way around the body. The right ventricle only pumps blood the shorter distance to the lungs.

Aorta: The largest artery in the body. It carries oxygenated blood away from the left ventricle to the rest of the body.

Vena cava: The largest vein. It carries deoxygenated blood from the body back into the right atrium of the heart.

Pulmonary artery: Carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. This is unusual because most arteries carry oxygenated blood.

Pulmonary vein: Carries oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the left atrium. Again, this is unusual because most veins carry deoxygenated blood.

Coronary arteries: Small arteries that branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood and nutrients.

Key Fact

The natural resting heart rate is controlled by a group of cells in the right atrium that act as a pacemaker. If the natural pacemaker is faulty, an artificial pacemaker — a small electrical device — can be implanted to correct irregular heart rhythms.

Types of Blood Vessel

The body contains three types of blood vessel, each adapted to its function.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. They have thick, elastic, muscular walls to withstand the surge of blood pumped with each heartbeat. Arteries branch into smaller vessels called arterioles, which eventually lead to capillaries.

Veins carry blood back towards the heart at low pressure. They have thinner walls than arteries and contain valves to prevent the backflow of blood. Skeletal muscles around veins help squeeze blood along.

Capillaries are microscopic vessels only one cell thick. They form networks that pass close to every cell in the body. Their thin walls allow the exchange of substances such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, glucose, and urea between the blood and surrounding tissues by diffusion.

Arteries: Thick muscular and elastic walls, small lumen, carry blood at high pressure away from the heart. No valves (except where they leave the heart).

Veins: Thinner walls with less muscle, larger lumen, carry blood at low pressure towards the heart. Contain valves to prevent backflow.

Capillaries: Walls just one cell thick, tiny lumen (red blood cells pass through in single file), allow substance exchange between blood and tissues.

Blood and Its Components

Blood is classified as a tissue. It consists of four main components, each with a specific role.

Plasma is the liquid, straw-coloured part of blood. It makes up about 55% of blood volume. Plasma transports dissolved substances around the body, including glucose and amino acids (to cells), carbon dioxide (to the lungs), urea (to the kidneys for excretion), hormones, and antibodies.

Red blood cells transport oxygen from the lungs to body tissues. They are biconcave in shape (like a flattened disc), which increases the surface area to volume ratio for efficient oxygen absorption. Red blood cells contain haemoglobin — a protein that binds with oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin, and releases it where oxygen concentration is lower in body tissues. Red blood cells have no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin.

White blood cells are part of the immune system. They defend the body against infection by engulfing pathogens (phagocytosis) or producing antibodies and antitoxins. Unlike red blood cells, white blood cells have a nucleus.

Platelets are small cell fragments (without a nucleus) that help blood to clot at the site of a wound. Platelets gather at the wound, triggering a cascade of reactions that form a mesh of fibrin threads, creating a scab. This prevents excessive blood loss and stops pathogens from entering.

Key Fact

Red blood cells are adapted for oxygen transport in three ways: biconcave shape (large surface area), packed with haemoglobin (binds oxygen), and no nucleus (more space for haemoglobin).

Coronary Heart Disease

Coronary heart disease (CHD) is a non-communicable disease. It occurs when layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow. This means the heart muscle receives less oxygen and glucose, which can lead to chest pain (angina) or, in severe cases, a heart attack.

Stents: A stent is a small mesh tube inserted into a narrowed coronary artery during surgery. It holds the artery open, restoring normal blood flow. Stents are effective and relatively low risk, but the artery can narrow again over time, and the patient needs to take blood-thinning medication.

Statins: These are drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels, slowing down the rate at which fatty deposits build up inside arteries. Statins must be taken long-term and can cause side effects such as headaches, muscle pain, and liver damage in some patients.

Faulty heart valves: If heart valves become faulty — either not opening fully or developing a leak — they can be replaced with biological valves (from human donors or other animals) or mechanical valves (made from metal or polymers). Faulty valves reduce the efficiency of blood flow through the heart.

Heart transplants and artificial hearts: In cases of complete heart failure, a donor heart (or heart and lungs) can be transplanted. Artificial hearts are sometimes used temporarily to keep patients alive while waiting for a transplant, or to allow a damaged heart time to rest and recover. They are not a permanent solution.

The specification requires you to evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of treating cardiovascular diseases by drugs, mechanical devices, or transplant. Stents are effective and quick but carry surgical risk and may need replacing. Statins are widely available and reduce cholesterol but must be taken daily and have side effects. Valve replacements restore normal blood flow but biological valves wear out and mechanical valves require lifelong blood-thinning medication. Transplants can save lives but depend on donor availability, require immunosuppressant drugs (increasing infection risk), and carry rejection risk. Artificial hearts reduce the risk of rejection and blood clots but are temporary, require a power supply, and can cause bleeding.

Key Fact

In coronary heart disease, fatty deposits narrow the coronary arteries, reducing oxygen supply to the heart muscle. Stents hold arteries open; statins reduce cholesterol to slow fatty build-up.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about blood vessels, always link structure to function — for example, “arteries have thick elastic walls because they must withstand high pressure.” For 6-mark “extended response” questions on coronary heart disease treatments, make sure you evaluate both advantages and disadvantages of each treatment, and reach a clear conclusion. Command words like “evaluate” require you to weigh up evidence and make a judgement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The heart is part of a double circulatory system — blood is pumped to the lungs then pumped again to the body. Know the four chambers, the four key blood vessels (aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein), and the coronary arteries.
  • Blood has four components: plasma (transports dissolved substances), red blood cells (carry oxygen via haemoglobin), white blood cells (fight infection), and platelets (clotting).
  • Coronary heart disease is caused by fatty deposits narrowing the coronary arteries. Treatments include stents, statins, valve replacements, transplants, and artificial hearts — each with specific advantages and disadvantages you must be able to evaluate.

lessons.title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues
lessons.description: Risk factors for non-communicable diseases, cancer types, and plant tissue transport systems.
lessons.content_html:
Health and Disease

Health is defined as a state of physical and mental well-being. It is not simply the absence of disease. Many factors affect health, including diet, stress, and life situations, and these can have a profound effect on both physical and mental well-being.

Diseases fall into two broad categories. Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread between organisms. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) cannot be passed from person to person and are often linked to lifestyle or genetic factors. Both types are major causes of ill health worldwide.

Key Fact

Different types of disease can interact. For example, viruses living in cells can trigger cancers, immune system defects increase susceptibility to infections, immune reactions caused by pathogens can trigger allergies such as asthma, and severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness.

Risk Factors for Non-Communicable Diseases

Risk factors are linked to an increased rate of a disease. They can be aspects of a person’s lifestyle, substances in their body, or substances in their environment. For some risk factors, a causal mechanism has been scientifically proven. For others, only a correlation has been identified.

The specification requires you to know several key risk factor links:

  • Diet, smoking, and exercise affect the risk of cardiovascular disease. A diet high in saturated fat raises blood cholesterol, which can lead to fatty deposits in arteries.
  • Obesity is a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes. Excess body fat can make cells resistant to insulin.
  • Alcohol affects the liver (causing cirrhosis) and brain function (impairing judgement and reaction times).
  • Smoking is a risk factor for lung disease and lung cancer. Tar in cigarettes contains carcinogens that damage lung tissue.
  • Smoking and alcohol during pregnancy affect unborn babies, causing low birth weight, premature birth, and foetal alcohol syndrome.
  • Carcinogens, including ionising radiation (such as UV light and X-rays), are risk factors for cancer.

Many non-communicable diseases are caused by the interaction of several factors rather than a single cause. Students must be able to discuss the human and financial cost of NCDs to individuals, local communities, nations, and globally.

Human cost: Reduced quality of life, pain, disability, shortened life expectancy, emotional impact on patients and families, mental health consequences such as depression and anxiety.

Financial cost: Increased NHS spending on treatment and long-term care, lost working days and reduced productivity, cost of medications and ongoing support, burden on social care services. Globally, NCDs account for the majority of healthcare expenditure in developed countries.

Cancer

Cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division. Normally, cell division is tightly controlled by genes. When these control mechanisms fail — due to mutations in DNA — cells can divide rapidly and form a mass called a tumour.

There are two types of tumour. Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells that are contained in one area, usually within a membrane. They do not invade other parts of the body and are not cancerous, though they can cause problems if they press on nearby organs.

Malignant tumours are cancers. Their cells invade neighbouring tissues and can spread to different parts of the body in the blood, where they form secondary tumours. This spread of cancer cells is what makes malignant tumours dangerous and potentially fatal.

Key Fact

Benign tumours = contained, do not spread, not cancer. Malignant tumours = invade other tissues, spread through blood, form secondary tumours, ARE cancer. The key distinction the exam tests is whether the tumour can spread (metastasise).

Scientists have identified both lifestyle risk factors (such as smoking, obesity, UV exposure, and drinking alcohol) and genetic risk factors for various types of cancer. Having a risk factor does not guarantee someone will develop cancer — it increases the probability.

Benign: Cells grow slowly, are contained within a membrane, do not spread to other tissues, are not usually life-threatening (unless they press on vital structures such as the brain).

Malignant: Cells grow rapidly, invade surrounding healthy tissue, can break away and travel in the blood, form secondary tumours at distant sites, can be life-threatening. Treatment may include surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy.

Plant Tissues

Just like animals, plants are organised into tissues, organs, and organ systems. A plant tissue is a group of similar cells working together to perform a specific function. The specification requires knowledge of five key plant tissues:

  • Epidermal tissue: Covers the outer surface of the plant. It produces a waxy cuticle on leaves to reduce water loss.
  • Palisade mesophyll: Found near the upper surface of the leaf. Packed with chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
  • Spongy mesophyll: Found below the palisade layer. Has air spaces to allow gases (carbon dioxide and oxygen) to diffuse through the leaf.
  • Xylem: Transports water and dissolved mineral ions from roots to stems and leaves. Composed of hollow, dead cells strengthened by lignin.
  • Phloem: Transports dissolved sugars from leaves to the rest of the plant. Composed of elongated living cells with pores in their end walls allowing cell sap to pass through.

Meristem tissue is found at the growing tips of shoots and roots. It contains rapidly dividing undifferentiated cells that can develop into any type of plant cell, enabling growth throughout the plant’s life.

Key Fact

The leaf is a plant organ. For the exam, you must know the tissues within it: epidermis (with waxy cuticle), palisade mesophyll (photosynthesis), spongy mesophyll (gas exchange), xylem and phloem (transport), and guard cells surrounding stomata (control gas exchange and water loss).

The Plant Organ System

The roots, stem, and leaves form a plant organ system for the transport of substances. Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the surface of a plant, mainly through open stomata in the leaves. As water evaporates from the leaf surface, more water is pulled up through the xylem from the roots — this continuous flow is called the transpiration stream.

The rate of transpiration is affected by four environmental factors: increasing temperature, decreasing humidity, increasing air movement (wind), and increasing light intensity all increase the rate of transpiration. Guard cells open and close the stomata to balance gas exchange for photosynthesis against water loss.

Translocation is the movement of dissolved sugars through phloem from the leaves (where sugars are made by photosynthesis) to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage. Unlike transpiration, translocation requires energy and moves substances in both directions.

Root hair cells are adapted for efficient uptake of water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport. Their long, thin extensions increase the surface area in contact with soil water.

Temperature: Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, so more evaporate from the leaf surface. Humidity: Lower humidity means a steeper concentration gradient between the inside of the leaf and the outside air, so water diffuses out faster. Air movement: Wind carries away water vapour from the leaf surface, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient. Light intensity: More light causes stomata to open wider for photosynthesis, allowing more water to escape.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on non-communicable diseases, always name the specific risk factor and link it to the specific disease (e.g. “smoking increases the risk of lung cancer because tar contains carcinogens”). For compare questions on tumours, structure your answer clearly: state the feature, describe it for benign, then describe it for malignant. For plant transport questions, don’t confuse xylem (water, up only, dead cells) with phloem (sugars, both directions, living cells).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health is complete physical and mental well-being. Risk factors (diet, smoking, alcohol, obesity, carcinogens) increase the chance of non-communicable diseases — many NCDs involve multiple interacting factors.
  • Benign tumours are contained and do not spread; malignant tumours invade tissues and spread via the blood to form secondary tumours. Both lifestyle and genetic factors affect cancer risk.
  • Xylem transports water upward (dead, hollow, lignin-strengthened cells); phloem transports sugars in both directions (living cells with pores). Transpiration rate increases with temperature, wind, light, and lower humidity.

Environmental factors like ionising radiation (UV, radon) are carcinogens that are not always within individual control. lessons.title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences
lessons.description: How pathogens cause disease and the body's physical and immune defences against infection.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Communicable Diseases?

A communicable disease is an illness caused by a pathogen — a microorganism that enters the body and causes infection. Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. They can spread between organisms by direct contact, by water, by air (droplet inhalation) or by vectors such as insects.

Once inside the body, bacteria and viruses reproduce rapidly. Bacteria release toxins that damage tissues and make us feel ill. Viruses work differently — they invade living cells, take over the cell’s machinery to make copies of themselves, and destroy the host cell in the process.

Key Fact

Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. The four types are bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. Bacteria produce toxins; viruses damage cells by reproducing inside them.

Viral Diseases

Measles is caused by a virus spread by inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs. Symptoms include fever and a red skin rash. Measles is a serious illness that can be fatal if complications arise, which is why most young children in the UK are vaccinated against it.

HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) initially causes a flu-like illness. It is spread by sexual contact or exchange of body fluids, such as sharing needles. Unless controlled with antiretroviral drugs, HIV attacks the body’s immune cells. Late-stage HIV infection is called AIDS — when the immune system is so damaged it can no longer fight other infections or cancers.

Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) is a widespread plant pathogen. It causes a distinctive “mosaic” pattern of discolouration on leaves, reducing photosynthesis and stunting the plant’s growth.

Salmonella is a type of food poisoning caused by bacteria. It is spread by eating contaminated food or food prepared in unhygienic conditions. Symptoms include fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea — caused both by the bacteria themselves and the toxins they secrete. In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against Salmonella to help control its spread.

Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted disease (STD) caused by a bacterium. Symptoms include a thick yellow or green discharge from the vagina or penis and pain when urinating. It was once easily treated with penicillin, but many antibiotic-resistant strains have now appeared. The spread of gonorrhoea can be reduced by using barrier methods of contraception such as condoms, and by treating infected individuals with antibiotics.

Rose black spot is a fungal disease of plants. Purple or black spots develop on leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early. This reduces photosynthesis and slows the plant’s growth. The fungus spreads through the environment by water or wind. It can be treated with fungicides or by removing and destroying affected leaves.

Malaria is caused by a protist pathogen. The malarial protist is spread by mosquitoes, which act as vectors — they carry the protist from person to person when they bite. Malaria causes recurrent episodes of fever and can be fatal. Its spread is controlled by preventing mosquitoes from breeding (draining stagnant water) and by using mosquito nets to avoid bites.

Human Defence Systems

The human body has two lines of defence against pathogens. The first is a set of non-specific defences — physical and chemical barriers that try to stop pathogens entering the body in the first place.

Key Fact

Non-specific defences include: the skin (acts as a physical barrier), the nose (hairs and mucus trap particles), the trachea and bronchi (lined with mucus and cilia that sweep trapped pathogens to the back of the throat), and the stomach (produces hydrochloric acid that kills most pathogens).

The Immune Response

If pathogens get past the non-specific defences, the body’s immune system is triggered. White blood cells are the key players in this response. They defend the body in three main ways:

1. phagocytosis — Some white blood cells (phagocytes) detect pathogens and engulf them. They surround the pathogen, take it into the cell and digest it with enzymes. This is a non-specific response — phagocytes attack any invading pathogen.

2. Antibody production — Other white blood cells (lymphocytes) recognise specific antigens on the surface of a pathogen. Each pathogen has unique antigens. The lymphocytes produce specific antibodies that lock onto these antigens and mark the pathogen for destruction. Antibodies are specific — each type only works against one particular pathogen.

3. Antitoxin production — Some white blood cells produce antitoxins that neutralise the toxins produced by bacteria, reducing the damage to tissues.

Key Fact

White blood cells defend the body by: (1) phagocytosis — engulfing and digesting pathogens, (2) producing antibodies that target specific antigens, and (3) producing antitoxins that neutralise bacterial toxins.

Different diseases require different prevention strategies. Good hygiene (handwashing, proper food preparation) reduces bacterial spread. Vaccination programmes protect against viral diseases like measles. Using barrier contraception prevents the spread of STDs like gonorrhoea and HIV. Destroying vectors — such as draining standing water where mosquitoes breed — helps control protist diseases like malaria. Isolating infected individuals and quarantine measures also reduce transmission of airborne diseases.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the exam, you may be asked to describe how a named disease is spread and prevented, or to explain the role of white blood cells. A common mistake is confusing antibodies with antitoxins — remember that antibodies target specific antigens on pathogens, while antitoxins neutralise the poisons (toxins) that bacteria release. For extended response questions on this topic, structure your answer by type of pathogen (virus, bacterium, fungus, protist) and give a named example for each.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists) cause communicable diseases and can spread by contact, air, water or vectors.
  • Non-specific defences (skin, nose, trachea, stomach acid) form the body’s first barrier against infection.
  • White blood cells fight infection through phagocytosis, antibody production and antitoxin production.

lessons.title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development
lessons.description: How vaccines trigger immunity, why antibiotics only kill bacteria, and how new drugs are tested.
lessons.content_html:
Overview

This lesson covers three closely linked topics: how vaccination protects individuals and populations, how antibiotics and painkillers are used to treat disease, and how new drugs are discovered, developed and tested before they reach patients.

These topics connect directly to the immune response you studied in the previous lesson. Vaccination uses the body’s own defence system, while antibiotics and other drugs work alongside it. Understanding the difference between preventing disease (vaccination), curing disease (antibiotics) and treating symptoms (painkillers) is essential for the exam.

How Vaccination Works

Vaccination involves introducing a small quantity of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body. These cannot cause the disease, but they carry the same antigens as the live pathogen. When the immune system detects these antigens, white blood cells respond by producing specific antibodies that match the pathogen’s antigens.

The crucial advantage of vaccination is immunological memory. After the initial immune response, the body retains memory lymphocytes that “remember” the pathogen’s antigens. If the same pathogen enters the body in the future, these memory cells trigger a much faster and stronger antibody response — destroying the pathogen before it can cause illness.

Key Fact

Vaccination introduces dead or inactive pathogens → white blood cells produce antibodies → memory lymphocytes remain in the body → if the same pathogen re-enters, antibodies are produced rapidly, preventing infection. The vaccine itself does not cure disease — it trains the immune system to respond.

When a large proportion of a population is vaccinated, the spread of the pathogen is significantly reduced because there are fewer people who can become infected and pass it on. This is called herd immunity. It protects people who cannot be vaccinated — such as very young babies, pregnant women, or people with weakened immune systems — because the pathogen cannot find enough hosts to spread through the population.

Vaccination programmes have been enormously successful: smallpox was completely eradicated by 1980 through a global vaccination campaign, and diseases like measles, polio and diphtheria have been dramatically reduced. However, if vaccination rates drop, herd immunity is lost and outbreaks can return.

Antibiotics and Painkillers

Antibiotics, such as penicillin, are medicines that kill infective bacteria inside the body. They have dramatically reduced deaths from bacterial diseases since their widespread use began in the 1940s. It is important to understand that specific bacteria must be treated by specific antibiotics — not all antibiotics work against all types of bacteria.

Key Fact

Antibiotics kill bacteria but cannot kill viruses. This is because viruses reproduce inside human cells. Destroying the virus would mean destroying the body’s own cells, which is why it is so difficult to develop drugs that target viruses without causing damage to body tissues. Painkillers treat the symptoms of disease (such as pain and fever) but do not kill pathogens.

Mutations in bacterial DNA can produce new strains that are antibiotic resistant. When antibiotics are used, non-resistant bacteria are killed but resistant ones survive. These resistant bacteria then reproduce, passing on the resistance gene. Over time, the population of resistant bacteria grows — a process driven by natural selection.

MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is a well-known example of an antibiotic-resistant strain. To reduce the development of resistant strains, three measures are essential:

  • Doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately — for example, not for viral infections or non-serious illnesses
  • Patients must complete their full course of antibiotics so all bacteria are killed and none survive to develop resistance
  • Agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted to prevent resistance developing in animal bacteria and transferring to humans

The development of new antibiotics is costly and slow, and is unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains. This is why preventing resistance is so critical.

Discovery and Development of Drugs

Traditionally, drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms. Three important historical examples are:

  • Digitalis — a heart drug originating from foxgloves
  • Aspirin — a painkiller originating from willow bark
  • Penicillin — discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 from the Penicillium mould

Today, most new drugs are synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry. However, the starting point may still be a chemical extracted from a plant or microorganism.

Before any new drug can be used on patients, it must be extensively tested for three things: toxicity (is it safe?), efficacy (does it work?) and dose (what is the right amount?). The testing process has two stages:

Preclinical testing is carried out in a laboratory. The drug is first tested on cells and tissues to check for toxicity, and then on live animals to see how it behaves in a whole organism. This stage identifies drugs that are too dangerous to test on humans.

Clinical trials use human volunteers. Very low doses are given at the start to check for safety. If the drug is found to be safe, further trials are carried out at higher doses to find the optimum dose — the amount that is most effective with the fewest side effects.

In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo — a substance that looks identical to the drug but contains no active ingredient. Neither the patient nor the doctor knows who has received the real drug and who has received the placebo. This eliminates bias and ensures that any improvement is genuinely caused by the drug, not by the patient’s belief that they are being treated.

Results from clinical trials are only published after they have been checked through peer review — scrutiny by other scientists — to ensure the methods were sound and the conclusions are valid.

Key Fact — Drug Testing Stages

Preclinical testing (cells, tissues, animals) → Clinical trials (healthy volunteers, then patients) → Low dose first, then optimum dose → Double blind trials with placebos to eliminate bias → Peer review before publication. New drugs are tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on vaccination, always explain the mechanism: dead/inactive pathogen → antibodies produced → memory cells remain → rapid secondary response. Do not just say “vaccines stop you getting ill.” For drug development questions, remember the three things drugs are tested for: toxicity, efficacy and dose. A common mistake is confusing antibiotics with painkillers — antibiotics kill bacteria, painkillers only treat symptoms. Neither works on viruses.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Vaccination introduces dead or inactive pathogens to stimulate antibody production and create memory lymphocytes. Immunising a large proportion of the population creates herd immunity, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.
  • Antibiotics kill bacteria (not viruses). Overuse and misuse drive antibiotic resistance through natural selection. MRSA is a key example. Painkillers treat symptoms but do not kill pathogens.
  • New drugs are tested for toxicity, efficacy and dose through preclinical testing (cells, tissues, animals) and then clinical trials (humans). Double blind trials with placebos eliminate bias, and results undergo peer review.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Respiration
lessons.description: Photosynthesis, limiting factors, aerobic and anaerobic respiration, and metabolism.
lessons.content_html:
Photosynthesis — The Key Reaction

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and algae make their own food. It takes place in the chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which is then used to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

The word equation is:

Key Fact

carbon dioxide + water ⟶ glucose + oxygen
In symbols: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O ⟶ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction — energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.

You must be able to recognise the chemical symbols CO₂, H₂O, O₂ and C₆H₁₂O₆. The exam may ask you to write the equation in words or symbols, or to identify photosynthesis as endothermic.

Rate of Photosynthesis

Several factors affect how fast photosynthesis occurs. The three main factors are light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, and temperature. The amount of chlorophyll also affects the rate — plants with fewer chloroplasts or yellow leaves photosynthesise more slowly.

Each of these factors can become a limiting factor. A limiting factor is whichever factor is in shortest supply at a given time. For example, on a bright sunny day, CO₂ concentration may be the limiting factor because there is plenty of light but not enough carbon dioxide for the plant to photosynthesise any faster.

Light intensity: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases — up to a point. Beyond that point, the graph levels off because another factor (such as CO₂ or temperature) becomes limiting. At very low light, photosynthesis stops entirely.

Carbon dioxide concentration: Increasing CO₂ concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis until something else becomes limiting. In greenhouses, farmers may add extra CO₂ to boost plant growth.

Temperature: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes. As temperature rises, the rate increases because molecules have more kinetic energy. However, above about 40–45°C, enzymes denature and the rate drops sharply to zero.

Chlorophyll: Plants affected by disease, mineral deficiency, or genetic conditions may have less chlorophyll, reducing the rate of photosynthesis.

Key Fact

Required Practical 6: You must know how to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using pondweed. Count oxygen bubbles or measure the volume of gas collected at different distances from a lamp. The independent variable is light intensity (distance from lamp) and the dependent variable is the rate of gas production.

Uses of Glucose

The glucose produced by photosynthesis is not just used for energy. Plants use it for several purposes:

Respiration: Glucose is broken down in respiration to transfer energy for life processes. Storage as starch: Glucose is converted into insoluble starch, which can be stored in leaves, roots, and tubers without affecting water balance. Storage as fats and oils: Seeds often store energy as lipids. Cellulose: Glucose molecules are joined together to make cellulose, which strengthens cell walls. Amino acids and proteins: Glucose is combined with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil to make amino acids, which are then built into proteins.

Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration is the process of breaking down glucose using oxygen. It happens continuously in every living cell — in both animals and plants. It is an exothermic reaction, meaning it transfers energy to the surroundings.

The equation for aerobic respiration is:

Key Fact

glucose + oxygen ⟶ carbon dioxide + water
In symbols: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ ⟶ 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
This is the reverse of the photosynthesis equation. Aerobic respiration transfers much more energy than anaerobic respiration.

The energy released by respiration is used for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, for movement, and for keeping warm. Respiration is not the same as breathing — breathing is the mechanical process that ventilates the lungs, while respiration is the chemical reaction inside cells.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration occurs when cells cannot get enough oxygen. Because the oxidation of glucose is incomplete, far less energy is transferred compared to aerobic respiration.

In animal muscles: glucose ⟶ lactic acid. The build-up of lactic acid causes muscles to become fatigued and stop contracting efficiently. An oxygen debt builds up — this is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the accumulated lactic acid in the liver, where it is converted back to glucose.

In plants and yeast: glucose ⟶ ethanol + carbon dioxide. This process is called fermentation and has important economic uses: brewing alcoholic drinks and making bread rise (CO₂ creates bubbles in dough).

Response to Exercise

During exercise, the body’s demand for energy increases. To supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood, the body responds by increasing heart rate, breathing rate, and breath volume (the volume of air in each breath).

If the muscles cannot get oxygen fast enough during vigorous exercise, anaerobic respiration takes over. Lactic acid accumulates in the muscles, causing fatigue and pain. After exercise, you continue to breathe heavily to repay the oxygen debt. The blood carries lactic acid to the liver, where oxygen is used to convert it back into glucose.

Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells. This is why you pant after sprinting — your body is taking in extra oxygen to break down the lactic acid in the liver. The heart rate and breathing rate remain elevated until the oxygen debt is repaid.

Metabolism

Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions in a cell or the body. The energy transferred by respiration drives these enzyme-controlled reactions. You need to know the key metabolic processes:

Building up (anabolic): Conversion of glucose to starch, glycogen, and cellulose. Formation of lipid molecules from one glycerol and three fatty acids. Use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids, then proteins. Breaking down (catabolic): Respiration itself (breaking glucose down for energy). Breakdown of excess proteins to form urea for excretion by the kidneys (deamination).

Key Fact

Metabolism links together many topics across the biology specification. Remember: respiration provides the energy for all metabolic reactions. Glucose ⟶ starch/glycogen/cellulose. Glycerol + 3 fatty acids ⟶ lipids. Glucose + nitrates ⟶ amino acids ⟶ proteins. Excess proteins ⟶ urea (excreted by kidneys).
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing aerobic and anaerobic respiration in the exam, set up a clear table or use structured paragraphs covering three aspects: whether oxygen is needed, the products, and the relative amount of energy transferred. For calculation questions on photosynthesis rate, remember that light intensity follows an inverse square relationship with distance — if you halve the distance from the lamp, light intensity quadruples. Always show your working for full marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Photosynthesis (endothermic) converts CO₂ + H₂O into glucose + O₂ using light energy in chloroplasts. Limiting factors are light intensity, CO₂ concentration, temperature, and chlorophyll.
  • Aerobic respiration (exothermic) transfers much more energy than anaerobic respiration. In muscles, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid and creates an oxygen debt; in yeast, it produces ethanol + CO₂ (fermentation).
  • Metabolism is the sum of all reactions in the body — powered by energy from respiration. Key examples include glucose ⟶ starch, glycerol + fatty acids ⟶ lipids, and excess proteins ⟶ urea.

lessons.title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease
lessons.description: Aseptic technique for culturing bacteria, zones of inhibition, and plant disease detection.
lessons.content_html:
Culturing Microorganisms

Bacteria are grown in laboratories for research, to test the effectiveness of antibiotics and disinfectants, and to study how diseases spread. To grow bacteria, scientists provide the nutrients and conditions they need to reproduce by binary fission — a process where one bacterium splits into two identical cells.

Bacteria can be grown in a nutrient broth (a liquid containing dissolved nutrients) or on agar gel plates. Agar is a jelly-like substance extracted from seaweed. When mixed with nutrients and poured into a Petri dish, it sets into a firm surface that bacteria can grow across, forming visible colonies.

Key Fact

Under ideal conditions, bacteria can divide by binary fission approximately every 20 minutes. Starting from one bacterium, this means there could be over 1 million bacteria after just 7 hours.

Aseptic Technique

When culturing bacteria, it is essential to prevent contamination by unwanted microorganisms. Aseptic technique is the set of precautions taken to ensure that only the desired bacteria grow on the agar plate. Contamination could introduce harmful pathogens or produce unreliable results.

1. Sterilise equipment: The Petri dish, agar, and all equipment must be sterilised before use. The inoculating loop is sterilised by passing it through a hot Bunsen burner flame until it glows red. This kills any bacteria already on the loop.

2. Allow the loop to cool: After sterilising, the inoculating loop must be allowed to cool in the air without touching any surfaces. Placing it on the bench would pick up contaminants.

3. Transfer the bacteria: The lid of the bacterial culture bottle is briefly removed and the neck of the bottle is passed through the Bunsen flame to kill any microorganisms around the opening. The cooled loop is dipped into the culture to pick up bacteria.

4. Inoculate the agar plate: The lid of the Petri dish is lifted slightly — not removed completely — and the bacteria are spread in a zigzag pattern across the agar surface. The lid is replaced quickly to minimise exposure to airborne microorganisms.

5. Seal and incubate: The Petri dish is secured with two pieces of tape (not sealed all the way round, to allow air in and prevent the growth of anaerobic pathogens). The plate is stored upside down to stop condensation dripping onto the colonies.

Key Fact

In school laboratories, agar plates are incubated at a maximum of 25°C. This is because higher temperatures (such as 37°C, used in industry) could encourage the growth of harmful human pathogens. At 25°C, bacteria still grow but dangerous species are less likely to thrive.

Investigating Antibiotics — Zones of Inhibition

One key application of culturing bacteria is the required practical that investigates the effect of antibiotics or disinfectants on bacterial growth. Different substances are compared by measuring how effectively they prevent bacteria from growing.

In this experiment, filter paper discs are soaked in different antibiotics or disinfectants and placed on an agar plate that has been inoculated with bacteria (a “bacterial lawn”). A control disc soaked in distilled water is also placed on the plate. After incubation, clear areas appear around the discs where the substance has killed or prevented bacterial growth. These clear areas are called zones of inhibition.

The larger the zone of inhibition, the more effective the antibiotic or disinfectant is against that particular type of bacterium. However, a large zone does not mean the substance is effective against all bacteria — it may be useless against a different species.

To calculate the area of a zone of inhibition, measure the diameter of the clear zone in mm, halve it to get the radius, and use the formula: \(area = πr^{2}\). If the zone is not perfectly circular, measure the diameter in two directions and use the mean.

A zone of inhibition has a diameter of 20 mm. The radius is 20 ÷ 2 = 10 mm. The area = π × 10² = 3.14 × 100 = \(314 mm^{2}\).

If the diameters measured in two directions were 20 mm and 18 mm, the mean diameter = (20 + 18) ÷ 2 = 19 mm. Radius = 9.5 mm. Area = π × 9.5² = 3.14 × 90.25 = \(283 mm^{2}\).

Plant Disease

Plants can be infected by a range of pathogens including viruses, bacteria, fungi, and insects. Plant disease can reduce crop yields and threaten food security, so detecting and identifying diseases early is critical.

Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV): A virus that causes a distinctive mosaic pattern of discolouration on the leaves. This reduces the amount of chlorophyll available for photosynthesis, stunting the plant’s growth.

Rose black spot: A fungal disease that causes purple or black spots on leaves. Infected leaves turn yellow and drop early, reducing photosynthesis. It spreads through water and wind.

Aphids: Aphids are small insects that feed on plant sap from the phloem. They weaken the plant by removing sugars and amino acids, and can act as vectors, transmitting viral diseases from one plant to another.

Detecting Plant Disease

Plant diseases can be detected in several ways. Gardeners, farmers, and scientists look for visible signs such as stunted growth, spots or lesions on leaves, areas of decay or rot, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration, and the presence of pests. These symptoms help narrow down the possible cause.

To confirm a diagnosis, scientists can use identification keys (dichotomous keys that guide users through a series of yes/no questions), testing kits that detect specific pathogens using monoclonal antibodies, or laboratory analysis including DNA testing or culturing the pathogen.

Ion Deficiency in Plants

Sometimes what looks like disease is actually caused by a mineral ion deficiency. Plants absorb mineral ions from the soil through their roots by active transport, and a shortage of key minerals produces distinctive symptoms.

Nitrate deficiency: Nitrate ions are needed to make amino acids and proteins. Without enough nitrate, the plant cannot grow properly and shows stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves (chlorosis). Magnesium deficiency: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll. Without enough magnesium, leaves turn yellow because chlorophyll cannot be produced, reducing photosynthesis.

Key Fact

Nitrate is needed for protein synthesis (making amino acids), so deficiency causes stunted growth. Magnesium is needed for chlorophyll production, so deficiency causes yellow leaves. Learn these two mineral deficiencies — they are commonly examined.

Plant Defence Responses

Plants cannot run away from threats, so they have evolved a range of physical, chemical, and mechanical defences to protect themselves against pathogens and herbivores.

Physical defences: Cellulose cell walls act as a barrier to pathogens. Tough, waxy cuticles on leaf surfaces prevent water loss and pathogen entry. Layers of dead cells on the outside of stems (bark) form a protective shield.

Chemical defences: Some plants produce antibacterial chemicals that kill invading pathogens — for example, mint and witch hazel produce antimicrobial substances. Others produce poisons to deter herbivores, such as the toxins in foxgloves (digitalis) and deadly nightshade. Some plants also produce chemicals that taste bitter or cause irritation.

Mechanical defences: Thorns and spines (e.g. on roses and cacti) deter animals from eating the plant. Leaves that droop or curl when touched (e.g. the mimosa plant) may deter insects. Some plants have hairy stems or leaves that make it difficult for insects to land or feed.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In AQA Biology exams, questions on culturing microorganisms often ask you to describe the aseptic technique step by step or explain why each step is necessary. Always link each step to preventing contamination. For zone of inhibition calculations, show your working clearly — write out the formula, substitute the values, and give units (mm²). Plant disease questions may ask you to compare physical, chemical, and mechanical defences, so learn at least one example of each type.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bacteria are cultured on agar plates using aseptic technique to prevent contamination. In schools, plates are incubated at a maximum of 25°C to avoid growing harmful pathogens.
  • Zones of inhibition show how effective an antibiotic or disinfectant is — a larger clear area means greater effectiveness against that specific bacterium. Area = πr².
  • Plants can be affected by pathogens (TMV, rose black spot, aphids) and mineral deficiencies (nitrate for stunted growth, magnesium for yellow leaves). They defend themselves through physical, chemical, and mechanical adaptations.
